The month's offerings average a solid 75/100 among critics, though reception varies considerably depending on each production's ambitions and execution.

Leading the pack is a revival of **Ragtime**, which earns critical acclaim for its timely resonance and commanding performances. Joshua Henry's work anchors a production that critics find both emotionally potent and relevant to contemporary conversations, proving that Terrence McNally, Lynn Ahrens, and Stephen Flaherty's 1998 musical still has plenty to say.

In a different register entirely, **Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York)** offers an intimate alternative to Broadway's typical spectacle. This British import succeeds through simplicity, with critics responding warmly to its sincere two-hander structure and modest romantic comedy charms—a reminder that not every Broadway show needs to be an epic to connect with audiences.

Meanwhile, **Chess** generates the most divided response. While critics universally praise the ABBA-penned score and the vocal firepower of Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit, and their co-star, questions about the production's overall coherence keep it from reaching the heights of its musical moments.

The range this month—from socially conscious period drama to contemporary rom-com to Cold War-era rock opera—reflects Broadway's ongoing effort to balance prestige revivals with fresh voices and proven crowd-pleasers. Whether you're drawn to powerful storytelling, intimate character work, or vocal pyrotechnics, March's slate offers clear entry points for different theatrical tastes.

# Best Broadway Shows from 2020

While that year's season was dramatically curtailed, the productions that did make it to the stage before the shutdown continue to resonate in discussions about the decade's most significant work.

Leading our rankings is a reimagined **Les Misérables** at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre, where critics largely embrace this grittier reboot of the beloved musical, even as some purists remain unconvinced by the darker approach. Close behind, **A Soldier's Play** earns widespread acclaim for its long-overdue Broadway debut—Charles Fuller's Pulitzer-winning drama proves its examination of race and power within a World War II-era army base remains urgently relevant in this stellar revival.

The year's other notable offerings present a study in contrasts. Laura Linney commands the stage in **My Name is Lucy Barton**, a solo performance that divides critics between those captivated by her luminous work and those who find the adaptation too slight for Broadway. Meanwhile, **Grand Horizons** delivers familiar but well-crafted boulevard comedy elevated by Jane Alexander and James Cromwell, and Ivo van Hove's radical **West Side Story** reimagining sparks passionate debate with its bold visual design and unconventional staging choices.

With an average critic score of 74/100 across these five productions, the class of 2020 demonstrates both artistic ambition and the enduring challenge of balancing innovation with audience expectations. Explore the full reviews and details below to discover which of these productions might still be worth revisiting in regional or touring productions.

Close behind, "The Phantom of the Opera" and the immersive "Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club" revival demonstrate the enduring power of musical theater, whether through Lloyd Webber's spectacular melodrama or Rebecca Frecknall's bold reimagining of the Weimar classic.

These productions collectively represent a pivotal moment when Broadway didn't just return—it returned with purpose, innovation, and artistic courage. This collection of five productions showcases the diversity of dramatic work that graced—however briefly—the stages before the industry-wide shutdown.

**Les Misérables** leads our rankings with its grittier reboot at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre, earning critical acclaim for reimagining the beloved musical's dramatic elements. The production demonstrates how classic material continues to find new resonance through bold directorial choices.

**A Soldier's Play** stands as a particular triumph, bringing Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama to Broadway for the first time in a revival that critics widely celebrate for its timeliness and stellar ensemble work. The production proves that some stories only grow more urgent with time, examining racial tensions within a World War II-era Army base with devastating relevance.

The remaining productions illustrate the range of theatrical voices active in 2020: Laura Linney's solo turn in **My Name is Lucy Barton** divides critics between admiration for her performance and questions about the adaptation itself, while **Grand Horizons** offers more traditional boulevard comedy elevated by veteran performers. Ivo van Hove's controversial **West Side Story** reimagining rounds out the list, polarizing audiences with its radical approach to the canonical material.

With an average critic score of 74/100 across these five productions, the class of 2020 represents solid, if not universally acclaimed, theatrical programming. Whether you're drawn to bold reinterpretations, long-awaited debuts, or intimate character studies, these productions offer multiple entry points into the year's dramatic landscape.

# Best Broadway Plays That Opened in 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that debuted in 2021 represent a remarkable chapter in theater history—a season of reopening after unprecedented shutdown, marked by both experimental boldness and the return of beloved spectacles.

Leading the critical pack is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama that continues to mesmerize audiences with Deirdre O'Connell's extraordinary lip-sync performance to a real interview with the playwright's mother. This daring theatrical experiment earns the highest marks among 2021 openings, proving that Broadway audiences embrace innovation alongside tradition.

The season's range is striking: from intimate verbatim dramas like **Is This a Room**, which transforms an FBI transcript into pulse-pounding theater, to the spectacular return of **The Phantom of the Opera** and the immersive reinvention of **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club**, which physically transformed the Playhouse Theatre into a nightclub experience. Sam Mendes' **The Lehman Trilogy** delivers epic storytelling across 150 years of American capitalism, while Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped **Company** offers a vital reimagining of Sondheim's masterwork.

The 2021 season also marks Broadway's intentional reopening with Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's **Pass Over**, a powerful statement about whose stories lead the industry forward. Meanwhile, accessible crowd-pleasers like the pop-concert musical **SIX** prove that Broadway's commercial appeal remains robust.

With an average critic score of 81 out of 100 across these ten productions, the class of 2021 demonstrates exceptional quality and remarkable diversity in form, content, and ambition. Whether you're drawn to experimental docudrama, reimagined classics, or spectacular musical entertainment, these productions offer compelling reasons to experience live theater.

# Best Broadway Plays That Opened in 2022

As we look back from March 2026, the 2022 Broadway season stands out as a remarkable period of theatrical achievement, with an impressive collection of critically acclaimed productions that continue to resonate with audiences today.

Leading the field is **Kimberly Akimbo**, the quirky musical that critics have embraced as a near-perfect blend of comedy and poignancy, earning the highest marks among this exceptional group. Close behind, **Into the Woods** demonstrates that stripped-down revivals can be just as powerful as lavish productions, with this Sondheim tribute capturing widespread critical praise for its stellar performances and crystalline vision. **A Strange Loop**, Michael R. Jackson's Pulitzer Prize-winning meta-musical, rounds out the top tier with its brazenly original and brutally honest exploration of identity and artistry.

What distinguishes this collection of ten shows is their remarkable consistency—averaging 83 out of 100 across critical reviews—and their diversity of voices and forms. The season brought back three Pulitzer Prize-winning plays (**Topdog/Underdog**, **Between Riverside and Crazy**, and **How I Learned to Drive**) alongside new Pulitzer winners (**A Strange Loop** and **Cost of Living**), demonstrating Broadway's commitment to both honoring theatrical legacy and championing contemporary voices. From Tom Stoppard's deeply personal **Leopoldstadt** to Jordan E. Cooper's provocative satire **Ain't No Mo'**, from Mike Birbiglia's masterful solo storytelling to multiple award-winning dramas, the range encompasses everything from intimate character studies to bold theatrical experiments.

Whether you're discovering these productions for the first time or revisiting familiar favorites, this guide offers a comprehensive look at a season that helped define modern Broadway's artistic landscape.

best-broadway-plays-2023.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2023

As of March 2026, the Broadway plays that premiered in 2023 continue to demonstrate the remarkable artistic vitality of that season, with productions earning an impressive average critic score of 82/100.

The year's theatrical landscape was defined by several triumphant revivals and bold new voices. Maria Friedman's staging of **Merrily We Roll Along** stands as the season's highest-rated play, finally vindicating Stephen Sondheim's notorious 1981 flop through what critics describe as an emotionally resonant interpretation that unlocks the show's long-obscured brilliance. Meanwhile, **Appropriate**, Branden Jacobs-Jenkins's searing family drama, earns widespread acclaim as a modern masterpiece, with Sarah Paulson leading what reviewers characterize as blistering ensemble work that excavates uncomfortable truths about inheritance and race.

The 2023 season also showcased Broadway's capacity for unexpected theatrical experiences, from the technically stunning **Stranger Things: The First Shadow**—a West End transfer that transcends its source material—to the long-overdue revival of **Purlie Victorious**, Ossie Davis's 1961 satire that critics find both hilarious and bracingly relevant for contemporary audiences. Other notable productions include Ben Platt and Micaela Diamond's powerhouse performances in **Parade**, the Pulitzer Prize-winning **Fat Ham**, and the immersive rock studio drama **Stereophonic**, which critics hail as a near-perfect theatrical experience.

This collection of ten productions represents a season that balanced artistic ambition with commercial appeal, revived overlooked classics, and championed diverse voices. Whether you're planning your next Broadway visit or reflecting on the theatrical highlights of 2023, these plays offer a compelling snapshot of American theatre at its most vital.

best-broadway-plays-2024.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in March 2026

As Broadway enters March 2026, the shows that premiered throughout 2024 continue to demonstrate exceptional staying power and critical acclaim. This collection of ten productions—ranging from intimate character studies to sweeping historical musicals—maintains an impressive average critic score of 83/100, reflecting a particularly strong year for theatrical storytelling.

Leading the field is **Stereophonic**, David Adjmi's acclaimed drama about a 1970s rock band in the studio, which critics consistently hail as a theatrical marvel for its authentic depiction of the creative process. The production's meticulous attention to period detail and raw emotional honesty have made it a critical darling. Close behind, **Operation Mincemeat** brings its grassroots energy from across the Atlantic, with reviewers praising the ensemble's inventive approach to this World War II espionage tale.

The diversity of this year's standouts is particularly noteworthy. **Maybe Happy Ending** offers audiences one of Broadway's most original musicals in recent memory—a tender robot love story that critics describe as unexpectedly moving. Meanwhile, Cole Escola's **Oh, Mary!** takes the opposite approach, delivering an irreverent, absurdist farce that reimagines Mary Todd Lincoln as a boozy, cabaret-obsessed narcissist to riotous effect.

From Audra McDonald's deeply personal interpretation of Mama Rose in **Gypsy** to the dance-driven innovation of **Illinoise**, these productions showcase the breadth of theatrical expression currently available on Broadway. Whether audiences seek emotional depth, historical insight, or pure entertainment, the class of 2024 continues to deliver compelling reasons to experience live theater.

best-broadway-plays-2025.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays

As Broadway moves into spring 2026, the plays that opened last year continue to demonstrate the enduring power of dramatic storytelling on stage. This season's strongest offerings span from bold revivals of American classics to intimate contemporary dramas, maintaining an impressive average critic score of 84/100 across ten productions.

Ivo van Hove's minimalist revival of **All My Sons** leads the field, earning widespread acclaim for its emotional intensity and exceptional ensemble work. The Dutch director's stark approach to Arthur Miller's family tragedy proves that stripped-down staging can amplify rather than diminish the text's power. Close behind, the 20th-anniversary revival of **The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee** reminds audiences why this quirky musical comedy became a beloved fixture, with critics praising its airtight writing and emotional depth.

Family entertainment finds sophisticated expression in **Paddington The Musical**, where a remarkably lifelike bear puppet has become a theatrical marvel that appeals to both children and adults. Meanwhile, contemporary playwrights make their mark with Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer-winning **English**, which explores language and identity with intelligence and sensitivity, and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins's **Purpose**, another searing family drama featuring the playwright's signature blend of sharp humor and piercing observation.

The season also showcases ambitious revivals of **Ragtime**, powered by Joshua Henry's commanding performance, and innovative new works like **Liberation**, Eliza Wohl's structurally complex feminist memory play. Whether you're drawn to classic American drama reimagined for contemporary audiences or bold new voices pushing theatrical boundaries, this season's plays offer compelling reasons to experience live theater.

best-broadway-plays-2026.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2026

March 2026 brings a notably lean opening schedule for new Broadway plays, with just one production making its debut this month. While the limited roster reflects the challenging economics facing straight plays on Broadway, the sole entry demonstrates the enduring appeal of well-crafted psychological drama.

**Bug** stands as the month's singular offering, marking the long-awaited Broadway premiere of Tracy Letts' 1996 psychological thriller. With a solid critic score of 74/100 across 35 reviews, the production earns mostly positive notices for its intense exploration of paranoia and delusion. Originally produced by Chicago's Red Orchid Theatre three decades ago, the play arrives on Broadway with renewed relevance, its themes of conspiracy and fractured reality resonating in contemporary discourse. Critics particularly praise the production's claustrophobic staging and committed performances, though some note the material's deliberately unsettling nature may not appeal to all theatergoers.

The sparse March schedule underscores a broader trend in commercial theater, where plays increasingly struggle to secure Broadway berths amid rising production costs and risk-averse producers. That **Bug** makes it to the Great White Way at all speaks to both the strength of Letts' reputation—bolstered by his Pulitzer Prize-winning **August: Osage County**—and the theater community's ongoing commitment to provocative, challenging work.

For audiences seeking substantive dramatic fare this month, **Bug** offers a compelling if confronting option that showcases the raw power of theatrical storytelling. Those planning their spring theater calendar should consider catching this production while monitoring announcements for upcoming play openings in the months ahead.
